newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU countries slammed for human rights abuse.
newsitem.headline: EU countries slammed for human rights abuse.

text.p: Greece came top of the list of European Union countries criticised by the European Parliament on Tuesday for human rights abuses in 1994.

According to a report by Spanish Conservative Laura de Esteban Martin, Greece was found wanting in 1994 in its treatment of detainees, prisoners, conscientious objectors, religious and ethnic minorities, and asylum-seekers.

The annually-produced report also slams Greece, along with Belgium, Britain and Ireland, for failing to ratify the European Convention on Human Rights protocol abolishing the death penalty except for acts committed in time of war.
Belgium continued to hand down death sentences for "non-exceptional" crimes too, the only EU country to do so.
De Esteban Martin said EU citizens' right to life also came under threat from continuing terrorist attacks in 1994, namely in Spain and Northern Ireland.
While her report roundly condemns terrorism and drugs gangs, it also criticises several member states for violating detainees' rights to a fair trial in 1994.
In fact, the European Court of Human Rights judged the Netherlands and France to have abused this right in four cases each, Britain and Greece in two cases each, and Italy and Portugal once each.

Although all the member states have signed the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment, Council of Europe reports on the situation in Portugal, Belgium and Greece in 1994 speak of detainees being ill-treated by police and deplorable prison conditions.
Britain refused to allow publication of a report on conditions in Northern Ireland, the Spanish Euro-MP's account says.

In a resolution, whose more controversial elements were adopted by the narrowest of margins, Euro-MPs said the EU's 15 member states must clean up their act in all these areas, as well as stepping up measures to combat child abuse and trafficking in human beings.

The EU assembly said it was also very concerned that EU governments' "legitimate desire" to reduce the number of unfounded asylum claims had led to the adoption of measures which blocked access to all asylum seekers, genuine or otherwise, with consequent fears for their safety.

Euro-MPs were particularly critical of the concept of "safe third countries", under which EU governments can refuse to consider asylum-seekers' claims if they have transitted through a "safe" non-EU country on their way to an EU state.
Greece, for example, which returns asylum seekers who transitted through Turkey and Germany, considers all its Central and East European neighbours to be safe, according to De Esteban Martin.
The assembly singled out Greece again - for prosecuting conscientious objectors, in some cases with prison sentences of up to four years, and failing to introduce civilian service.
Euro-MPs attacked London for denying civil servants the right to join a trade union, and Athens for restricting freedom of expression on delicate issues such as relations with Macedonia.
They said Athens was wrong to oblige citizens to state their religious confession on their identity papers. Religious minorities fear this might lead to discrimination.
There was much concern about the rise in racism and xenophobia in the EU, with particularly nasty incidents in Italy, Germany and Greece in 1994.

But Euro-MPs stepped back from insisting that anyone who incited racial hatred or advocated racial discrimination should be ineligible to stand for public office, including membership of the European Parliament.
Among the 31 Euro-MPs in the non-aligned group are 14 deputies from the French and Belgian National Fronts and Belgium's Vlaams Blok, whose central plank is racial exclusion.
